issues.legal_issue: A possession decree may be entered on admissions when the landlord–tenant relationship and termination of a tenancy outside rent-control protection are not in dispute.
material_facts: The suit sought possession from a tenant whose rent placed the tenancy outside rent-control protection.
The tenant’s pleadings admitted the landlord–tenant relationship and service of a termination notice.
The trial court entered a possession decree on admissions, which the Supreme Court affirmed.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was justified in decreeing possession on admissions because the landlord–tenant relationship and termination of the tenancy were admitted.
issues.legal_principle: Order XII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits judgment on admissions in pleadings or otherwise when they suffice to grant the relief sought. In a possession suit against a tenant whose tenancy is not protected by rent-control law, the landlord must establish the landlord–tenant relationship and termination by lapse of time or notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Whether an admission is clear and unequivocal depends on the facts of each case, as explained in Jeevan Diesels & Electricals Ltd. v. Jasbir Singh Chadha; see also Karam Kapahi v. Lal Chand Public Charitable Trust and Charanjit Lal Mehra v. Kamal Saroj Mahajan.

predicates.possession_suit_against_unprotected_tena: The proceeding is a landlord’s suit for possession against a tenant whose tenancy is not protected by rent-control law.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship_admitted: The tenant’s pleadings or other statements admit the landlord–tenant relationship.
predicates.tenancy_termination_admitted: The tenant’s pleadings or other statements admit that the tenancy ended by lapse of time or service of a termination notice.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks possession from an unprotected tenant and both the relationship and termination are admitted, a possession decree on admissions is available.

issues.legal_issue: An admitted tenancy relationship is not negated for purposes of possession by disputes about the premises’ use, an unregistered lease document, or alterations to the premises.
material_facts: The tenant did not deny execution of the lease document, admitted the agreed rent, and occupied the premises under the landlord.
The tenant disputed whether the premises were let for residential or commercial use and asserted that the lease document did not contain the parties’ actual terms.
The tenant also claimed to have constructed or altered the superstructure, but the tenancy was not protected by rent-control law.
issues.conclusion: The pleadings admitted the landlord–tenant relationship; the dispute about use, the lease document’s registration, and structural changes did not prevent a possession decree.
issues.legal_principle: For possession, the relevant question is whether the landlord–tenant relationship is admitted. The premises’ residential or commercial use may bear on mesne profits but not on possession; structural changes do not alter the nature of possession held under the tenancy. The Court applied Order XII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and its fact-specific approach to admissions, as discussed in Jeevan Diesels & Electricals Ltd. v. Jasbir Singh Chadha.

predicates.possession_suit_against_unprotected_tena: The proceeding is a landlord’s suit for possession against a tenant whose tenancy is not protected by rent-control law.
predicates.lease_execution_admitted: The tenant’s pleadings do not deny that the parties executed the lease document.
predicates.tenant_occupies_under_landlord: The tenant entered and continues to occupy the premises under the landlord, even if the tenant disputes the premises’ use or claims to have altered its structures.

issues.definition: In an unprotected-tenancy possession suit, admitted execution and occupation under the landlord establish the admitted relationship for possession despite disputes about use or alterations.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s challenge to the validity of a termination notice does not deny its service when the tenant admits receipt and contests only its legal sufficiency.
material_facts: The tenancy was treated as a month-to-month tenancy because there was no registered lease securing a fixed term.
The tenant did not deny service of the notice, but pleaded that it did not comply with the statutory requirements for termination.
The notice was in the record, and the Supreme Court found no illegality that made it ineffective.
issues.conclusion: The tenant admitted receipt of the notice by challenging its validity rather than denying service, and the notice was not legally defective.
issues.legal_principle: A month-to-month tenancy may be terminated by notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. A pleading that a notice is invalid, without denying its receipt, admits service; the Court found that the notice in this case was not illegal. The admission could support judgment under Order XII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: possession_suit_against_tenant and notice_received and only_notice_validity_disputed and notice_not_legally_defective

predicates.possession_suit_against_tenant: The proceeding is a landlord’s suit seeking possession from a tenant.
predicates.notice_received: The tenant received the landlord’s notice terminating the tenancy.
predicates.only_notice_validity_disputed: The tenant contests the notice’s legal sufficiency but does not deny receiving it.
predicates.notice_not_legally_defective: The notice is not legally defective so as to be ineffective.

issues.definition: When a tenant in a possession suit received a notice, disputes only its validity, and the notice is not defective, service and effective termination are admitted.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant is estopped from denying the landlord’s title at the commencement of the tenancy when the tenant’s challenge is based on a title defect predating that tenancy.
material_facts: The tenant asserted that the property had vested in a local body under an order made before the tenancy began.
The tenant entered the tenancy under the landlord after that order and then challenged the landlord’s title on the basis of the earlier order.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was estopped from challenging the landlord’s title at the commencement of the tenancy, so that challenge did not defeat the possession claim.
issues.legal_principle: Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, estops a tenant from denying that the landlord had title to the property when the tenancy began. The principle applies where the challenged title predates the tenancy and the tenant accepts the claimant as landlord. The Court relied on Mangat Ram v. Sardar Mehartan Singh, Anar Devi v. Nathu Ram, Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath, and the Privy Council decision in Krishna Prasad v. Baraboni Coal Concern Ltd.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks to evict a person occupying property as a tenant.
predicates.tenant_accepted_landlord_as_lessor: The occupant entered or continued the tenancy by accepting the claimant as landlord.
predicates.title_challenge_predates_tenancy: The tenant’s challenge to the landlord’s title rests on a claimed defect that existed before the tenancy began.

issues.definition: In a tenant eviction proceeding, a tenant who accepted the claimant as landlord cannot deny title at the start of the tenancy on the basis of a defect predating it.
